rv.q: That truly dazzling feat of theatrical alchemy — which required respect, delicacy and guts — has resulted in far and away the best musical production of the current Broadway season.
Broadway’s ending its season with a sensational revival of “Pippin” — a thrilling piece of eye-popping razzle dazzle filled with daredevil acrobatics.
This new 'Pippin' is a circus stunner, a Broadway musical that has been reimagined as a breathtaking spectacle of acrobatic wizardry.
Here, in all its grand and dubious glory, is musical-theater showmanship at its best, a thrilling evening of art and craftiness spiked with ambivalence about the nature of enthrallment.
No matter how one feels about Stephen Schwartz's sappy 1972 hit, this production pumps up the facile material with nonstop, fearless brainstorms.
This production has done the same.
Massively, almost overwhelmingly entertaining, even if its audacious razzle-dazzle doesn't mask the limitations of its book.
Pippin reliably provides the kind of Broadway glow that’s impossible to forget and irreproducible elsewhere.
You can just sit back and let this exhaustingly energetic team work you over until you’re either all tingly or all numb.
Ms. Paulus’s production, which originated earlier this season at the Theatre in Cambridge, Mass., is a knock-’em-dead extravaganza meant to “revive” the show in every sense of the word.
The result is a combination of epic theater, burlesque and soulful spectacle that recaptures the show's shiny allure and its poignance while making it seem entirely fresh.
The final show to open before Tony Awards consideration, “Pippin” punctuates the Broadway season with a big, bold exclamation point.

This is not what Bob Fosse had in mind in 1972, when he turned Stephen Schwartz and Roger O. Hirson's youthful commedia dell'arte musical into something darker, sexier, more mysterious and decidedly grown-up.
It's been said that a musical has to have at least three 'wow' moments to really grab an audience. Well, the Diane Paulus-directed revival of the 1972 musical Pippin has at least seven.
With a little more ease, the revival might be a tad more genuinely charming than this nonstop whirl of entertainment that at times seems more distracting than diverting.

cn.t: Critics largely embrace this circus-infused revival as thrilling spectacle, praising Diane Paulus's inventive staging and eye-popping acrobatics that breathe fresh life into Schwartz's 1972 musical, though some find the thin material overwhelmed by razzle-dazzle.

vs.sum: The Music Box Theatre offers excellent sightlines from most seats, making it ideal for intimate dramas, though sound quality can vary. The theater's charming Georgian-inspired design adds to its ambiance, while comfort and facilities are average for a Broadway venue.
